newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF URGES BULGARIA TO SPEED STRUCTURAL REFORM.
newsitem.headline: IMF URGES BULGARIA TO SPEED STRUCTURAL REFORM.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Monday urged Bulgaria to speed up privatisation to fund a high budget deficit and sustain a currency board system designed to stabilise its troubled economy.

"It is very important to get the currency board functioning well and concentrate on the structural reforms, getting the privatisation process continuing and not slackening the pace," said Johannes Wijndholds, IMF executive director for the group of countries including Bulgaria.

Further IMF lending under a 510 million standby agreement sealed in April is hinged on Bulgaria meeting World Bank restructuring targets, of which 80 percent have been completed so far, said the bank.

A World Bank mission is due to arrive in Sofia in the second half of June to evaluate Bulgaria's performance. If World Bank targets are met the country stands to receive a 170 million structural adjustment loan in July.
Bulgaria moved a step closer to launching a currency board on July 1 after agreeing with the IMF on this year's draft budget frame a week ago and announced a fixed lev/mark rate of 1,000.

Speaking after meeting Prime Minister Ivan Kostov, Wijnholds said the peg rate and currency were well chosen and praised the government for dramatically curbing inflation, reducing interest rates and stabilising the lev.

"I feel quite optimistic after my talk with Prime Minister Kostov. Very important measures have been taken...Confidence is returning rapidly to Bulgaria under this excellent economic programme," Wijnoholds told reporters.
Bulgaria last week restructured its central bank to operate under the currency board system into three major departments -- Issue, Banking and Bank Supervision.
Parliament is expected to appoint a new central bank governor on Wednesday after amendments restructuring the central bank come in force on Tuesday.
Once preparations for the currency board and restructuring targets are completed, the IMF is expected to disburse a second 130 million tranche in July, said Wijnholds.

The second tranche is also linked to meeting several targets aimed at deregulating trade and boosting investment, which include approval of the 1997 budget, increase of Value Added Tax registration threshold to 50,000 and increase penalties and interest on outstanding tax liabilities in line with inflation.

Other targets include removal of bank privatisation barriers, amend the commercial law to allow banks and companies to hold their capital denominated in foreign currency, eliminate the existing restriction on repatriation of profits of small enterprises.
Bulgaria is also expected to remove price controls and export bans on fuels and eliminate the system of margin controls on farm products by July.
Wijnholds said a 6.2 percent draft budget deficit would not endanger the currency board as long as it was funded from privatisation proceeds and external lending. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
